verifications.claim_text: Experimental evidence on accuracy comes from Bonilla López et al. (2018), who randomly assigned low-intermediate EFL writers (N = 139) to four feedback conditions and a self-correction control.
verifications.evidence_quote: Low intermediate EFL writers (N = 139) were randomly assigned to four experimental conditions (direct corrections on grammatical errors, metalinguistic codes on grammatical errors, direct corrections on grammatical and non-grammatical errors, or metalinguistic codes on grammatical and non-grammatical errors) and a control group (self-correction).
verifications.explanation: Every proposition in the claim is stated in the source. The abstract reports that "Low intermediate EFL writers (N = 139) were randomly assigned to four experimental conditions (direct corrections on grammatical errors, metalinguistic codes on grammatical errors, direct corrections on grammatical and non-grammatical errors, or metalinguistic codes on grammatical and non-grammatical errors) and a control group (self-correction)." Section 4.1 confirms the same: 139 participants, mean proficiency "lower intermediate", "randomly assigned to five groups" including "a control group (n = 27)" described in 4.3 as "a self-correction (i.e., control) group (hereafter SC), where learners did not receive any corrections in their text." The study's accuracy outcomes (immediate and long-term grammatical and non-grammatical accuracy) are the paper's central results, so the claim that accuracy evidence comes from this study is supported. The only element not literally in the chunks is the publication year 2018, which is a bibliographic detail of the citing paper rather than a substantive proposition about the study; it is treated as peripheral and does not affect the verdict.

verifications.evidence_quote: a long-term advantage (i.e., four weeks after feedback provision) was only evident for direct corrections
verifications.explanation: The claim reproduces the abstract's own summary almost verbatim: "a long-term advantage (i.e., four weeks after feedback provision) was only evident for direct corrections." The four-week timing is confirmed by the design description ("Four weeks later, in session 5 students had 30 minutes to write a new text (delayed posttest)"), and the restriction to direct corrections is confirmed both by the abstract and by the discussion ("in the long term non-grammatical accuracy was durable with direct corrections only whereas grammatical issues maintained the feedback effect with either feedback type—although direct corrections proved superior"). The discussion's qualification that grammatical accuracy was maintained by either feedback type is a nuance about grammatical vs. non-grammatical outcomes, but the paper's own stated overall conclusion is the one the claim reports, so no assertion is contradicted or absent.

verifications.claim_text: learners reported significantly lower cognitive load when revising after direct corrections on grammatical errors than after metalinguistic codes on grammatical and non-grammatical errors
verifications.evidence_quote: the cognitive load imposed by revision after DCF+G was significantly lower than that after ME+GN (p < 0.001, SE = 0.350)
verifications.explanation: The central assertion — that reported cognitive load after revision following direct corrections on grammatical errors (DCF+G) was significantly lower than after metalinguistic codes on grammatical and non-grammatical errors (ME+GN) — is stated directly in section 5.4: "the cognitive load imposed by revision after DCF+G was significantly lower than that after ME+GN (p < 0.001, SE = 0.350)", and Table 3 lists "***ME+GN > DCF+G 1.91 [0.95, 2.88]" under Perceived cognitive load. The descriptive means (DCF+G = 4.76 vs. ME+GN = 6.68) are consistent with the direction. The peripheral assertions (learners' self-reported mental effort on Paas's scale; the two specific feedback conditions) are also supported by the methods and results sections. No contradiction and no hedge removal.

verifications.claim_text: The authors acknowledge they could not employ an online physiological measure of cognitive load, so this self-report finding warrants caution (Bonilla López et al., 2018).
verifications.evidence_quote: Besides, although this study was a first step into examining the cognitive load imposed by comprehensive CF, we were unable to  employ an online physiological measure.
verifications.explanation: The central assertion is supported: in the Limitations section the authors state "although this study was a first step into examining the cognitive load imposed by comprehensive CF, we were unable to  employ an online physiological measure," and Note 4 confirms that "The instructional context of this study prevented us from employing the latter" (physiological measures). The peripheral assertion that this limitation means the self-report finding "warrants caution" is not stated in the source: the authors instead frame the limitation as a call for future research ("to determine to what extent our findings hold under other conditions, a future research agenda may want to look into the cognitive load of feedback with a measure of eye activity") and defend the mental-effort scale as "widely adapted given its proven validity, unobtrusiveness, and easy availability." The general caution statement in the paper ("caution must be exercised when interpreting its findings") is attributed to the EFL learning-to-write/writing-to-learn setting, not to the absence of an online physiological measure. Hence the status is needs_nuance.

verifications.explanation: The central assertion — that reported cognitive load after revision following direct corrections on grammatical errors (DCF+G) was significantly lower than after metalinguistic codes on grammatical and non-grammatical errors (ME+GN) — is stated directly in section 5.4: "the cognitive load imposed by revision after DCF+G was significantly lower than that after ME+GN (p < 0.001, SE = 0.350)", and Table 3 lists "***ME+GN > DCF+G 1.91 [0.95, 2.88]" under Perceived cognitive load. The descriptive means (DCF+G = 4.76 vs. ME+GN = 6.68) are consistent with the direction. The peripheral assertions (learners' self-reported mental effort on Paas's scale; the two specific feedback conditions) are also supported by the methods and results sections. No contradiction and no hedge removal.

verifications.claim_text: In a survey of 70 students in a university ESL program in the southwestern United States, students favoured direct correction with metalinguistic explanations (215/447, 48.10%), followed by direct correction alone (111/447, 24.83%) (Liu and Wu, 2019).
verifications.evidence_quote: Seventy students from a university ESL program in the southwestern U.S. participated in the study.
verifications.explanation: Every proposition in the claim is stated in the source. The participant description matches: "Seventy students from a university ESL program in the southwestern U.S. participated in the study." The central ranking and counts match verbatim: "In general, students favored direct correction in conjunction with metalinguistic explanations (215/447, 48.10%) followed by direct correction without metalinguistic explanations (111/447, 24.83%)." The claim's "direct correction alone" is the source's "direct correction without metalinguistic explanations," the same measure. No assertion is contradicted or absent, and no hedge is removed.

verifications.claim_text: Their descriptive, non-randomised questionnaire design limits inference, and the authors themselves note the data are necessarily descriptive (Liu and Wu, 2019).
verifications.evidence_quote: Since this is not an experimental study but one that tapped into an existing pool of students and available teachers, data collected from such limited, non-randomized sources are necessarily descriptive.
verifications.explanation: The central assertion — that the authors themselves describe their data as necessarily descriptive — is stated verbatim in the Limitations section: "Since this is not an experimental study but one that tapped into an existing pool of students and available teachers, data collected from such limited, non-randomized sources are necessarily descriptive." The peripheral assertions are also supported: the design is a questionnaire survey of an existing pool of students and available teachers (non-randomised, non-experimental), and the authors state that the observed patterns "are context-specific and may not reflect student and teacher beliefs in a drastically different demographic and educational environment," i.e., inference is limited. No assertion is contradicted and no hedge is removed.

verifications.claim_text: observed a very limited range of revision operations in a second draft, with only seven of 35 errors corrected properly, and reported that automated feedback tended to highlight rather than correct errors
verifications.evidence_quote: We found a very limited range of revision operations in the second draft and out of 35 errors seven were corrected properly.
verifications.explanation: All three propositions are stated in the source. The study reports for David (AWE feedback) that "We found a very limited range of revision operations in the second draft and out of 35 errors seven were corrected properly", and in the comparison of feedback types it states "AWE feedback tended to highlight, rather than correct, student errors". The claim's "only seven of 35 errors corrected properly" matches the source's "out of 35 errors seven were corrected properly" exactly, and the "highlight rather than correct" wording reproduces the source's phrasing. No assertion is contradicted or absent.
